Given the absence of hypotension, tachycardia, orthostatic signs, peripheral edema, or heart failure signs, she appears clinically euvolemic. Urine osmolality of 334 mOsm/kg (>100) indicates continued ADH activity (i.e., inability to appropriately dilute the urine). Urine sodium of 45 mEq/L (>40) in a euvolemic patient points away from hypovolemia (where urine Na is typically low unless diuretics are used) and supports a diagnosis of euvolemic hyponatremia due to inappropriate ADH activity. Common causes include SIADH from malignancy (e.g., small cell lung cancer in a smoker), pulmonary or CNS disorders, or medication-induced (thiazides, SSRIs, etc.). There is no fever, focal neuro deficit, or other acute findings to suggest an alternative acute neurologic cause. Adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism can mimic SIADH and should be excluded with appropriate testing, but the initial laboratory pattern and clinical exam most strongly support SIADH causing symptomatic hyponatremia and acute confusion.

DIAGNOSIS: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) causing euvolemic hyponatremia.
